overview: Scelidosaurus harrisonii is one of the earliest armoured dinosaurs — an Early Jurassic ornithischian from the Charmouth Mudstone Formation of Dorset, England (~193 Ma). At about four metres, it bore rows of bony scutes (osteoderms) embedded in the skin along its back — the most complete armoured dinosaur from the Early Jurassic. Its exact position as either an early thyreophoran (Stegosauria/Ankylosauria ancestor) or a basal ornithischian outside Thyreophora is debated.

Scelidosaurus is historically significant as the first complete dinosaur skeleton to be described in scientific detail, predating the complete Iguanodon material from Belgium. Richard Owen described it in 1861 from marine sediment — the animal had drifted out to sea after death and been preserved in limestone nodules on the Jurassic coast.

fossilSites.name: Charmouth Mudstone Formation
fossilSites.note: Early Jurassic (Sinemurian) marine mudstones preserving the Scelidosaurus holotype — deposited by offshore carcass drift.

articles.title: Discovery and Owen's description
articles.body: Scelidosaurus was found in marine Jurassic cliffs near Charmouth, Dorset, in the 1850s. Richard Owen described it in 1861 as the first complete dinosaur known to science — a milestone given that Iguanodon and Megalosaurus were known only from fragments at the time. The marine preservation is explained by the carcass floating out to sea before sinking and being buried.

articles.title: Armour and taxonomy
articles.body: The osteoderms of Scelidosaurus are varied: keeled scutes, oval knobs and smaller granular elements. The arrangement and diversity of these armour elements is reminiscent of ankylosaur armour, leading most phylogenetic analyses to place Scelidosaurus as a basal thyreophoran ancestral to or sister to Ankylosauria. A minority view places it outside Thyreophora entirely.

articles.title: Early Jurassic context
articles.body: The Early Jurassic was a time of rapid dinosaurian diversification following the end-Triassic mass extinction. Scelidosaurus represents the early evolution of armoured herbivores in a lineage that would eventually produce the massively armoured ankylosaurs and the plated stegosaurs. Its modest size (4 m) and basic armour contrast with the elaborate defences of its much later relatives.

fossilRecord.material: Several partial to near-complete articulated skeletons.
fossilRecord.paleo: Early Jurassic nearshore marine environment — the Dorset specimens were apparently washed out to sea after death.
fossilRecord.evidence: Rows of scutes along the back and primitive thyreophoran skeletal features document its position near the base of the armoured dinosaur radiation.

record.mya: late Sinemurian, about 195-193 million years ago
record.description: Scelidosaurus harrisonii was an early armoured ornithischian from the Charmouth Mudstone Formation of Dorset, known from several skeletons including a nearly complete skull and postcranium.
facts: Modern redescription places it near the base of Thyreophora rather than securely inside Ankylosauria.
Its osteoderms and spikes are directly preserved, although colour and keratin coverings are unknown.

presentation.heroLead: A four-legged, armour-plated plant-eater from the Jurassic coast of Dorset, and one of the most completely known early armoured dinosaurs anywhere.

animalParagraphs: Scelidosaurus was a heavily built, low-slung ornithischian about four metres long, with a small head, a long tail and a body walled with rows of bony plates. Its fossils come from the marine mudstones of Charmouth, where carcasses washed out to sea and settled in fine sediment that preserved several skeletons in articulation.

The skull carried a horny beak and rows of leaf-shaped teeth suited to cropping and simple slicing of foliage rather than grinding. The jaw joint sat level with the tooth rows and the wear on the teeth is modest, suggesting a simple up-and-down bite on low-growing plants.

Rows of keeled osteoderms ran along the neck, back, flanks and tail, with a distinctive three-pointed cluster behind each ear, all preserved in place on the best skeletons. The limbs were sturdy and the forelimb relatively long, indicating an animal that habitually walked on all fours, although young animals may have been more lightly built.
animalHighlights: Rows of keeled bony plates are preserved in their natural positions along the neck, body and tail.
A three-pronged cluster of osteoderms behind each side of the skull is unique to Scelidosaurus.
Sturdy limbs and a long forelimb indicate a habitual four-legged walker, the earliest well-documented example among ornithischians.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Leaf-shaped teeth and a beak indicate browsing on low vegetation. The particular plants are not preserved and there is no grinding dentition.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Forelimb length and robust limb bones show weight-bearing on all four legs. A bipedal stance in juveniles is inferred rather than observed.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The lectotype and the Bristol skeleton give length directly; mass is estimated from limb dimensions and body reconstructions.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The osteoderms and small skin ossicles are preserved in position, but the keratin sheaths, skin colour and pattern are not.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Charmouth, near Lyme Regis, Dorset, England

locality.name: Charmouth
locality.note: Charmouth Mudstone Formation, Black Ven cliffs. All secure specimens come from a short stretch of the Jurassic Coast between Charmouth and Lyme Regis.

presentation.classificationSummary: Scelidosaurus is an early thyreophoran, the armoured group that later gave rise to stegosaurs and ankylosaurs. The recent redescription places it near the base of Thyreophora, outside both later groups, rather than within Ankylosauria as some earlier analyses suggested.

related.reason: Compare with a smaller, lightly armoured Early Jurassic thyreophoran from North America.
Compare with a fragmentary early armoured ornithischian of similar age from Germany.
Compare with an early stegosaur that shows the next stage of thyreophoran armour.

questions.title: Which type specimen counts?
questions.copy: Owen first attached the name to a theropod knee joint, and a skull-and-skeleton lectotype had to be designated in 1994 so that the name applies to the armoured animal we recognise today.

questions.title: Ankylosaur or something earlier?
questions.copy: Scelidosaurus was long treated as a primitive ankylosaur. The full redescription argues for a position near the base of Thyreophora, but the placement still depends on which characters are scored.

questions.title: Were the plates covered in horn?
questions.copy: The bone cores of the osteoderms are preserved, and a keratin sheath is likely by comparison with living reptiles, but the covering itself has not been found.

review.ageReviewNote: Ammonite zonation places the Dorset material in the upper Sinemurian, approximately 195-193 Ma on the current time scale.

specimens.name: Lectotype
specimens.note: Near-complete skull and skeleton with armour in place, collected by James Harrison at Charmouth and described by Owen in 1861; designated lectotype in 1994.

specimens.name: Referred adult skeleton
specimens.note: Second near-complete skeleton from Charmouth used extensively in the 2020–2021 redescription.

specimens.name: Referred juvenile
specimens.note: Partial skeleton of a young individual.

panel.headline: Several articulated skeletons with the armour still in place.
panel.standfirst: Scelidosaurus is known from a near-complete lectotype skull and skeleton, a second near-complete adult in Bristol, a well-preserved private specimen found in 2000, and partial juveniles, all from the Charmouth Mudstone of Dorset.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented in articulated skeletons from more than one individual, with the dermal armour preserved in natural position and juveniles known alongside adults.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The lectotype preserves the skull with lower jaws, the complete vertebral column, both girdles, all four limbs and the osteoderms in place. The Bristol skeleton and the Charmouth specimen repeat most of this anatomy, and juvenile material in Cambridge and London records earlier growth stages.
knownRemains.note: All material comes from one formation on one stretch of coast, so geographic range and variation through time cannot be assessed.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Complete skull and lower jaws in the lectotype and Bristol specimen, with beak-bearing snout, full tooth rows and the paired osteoderm cluster behind the skull.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete articulated cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series with ribs, ossified tendons and tail chevrons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Shoulder and pelvic girdles, forelimbs and hindlimbs with hands and feet, from adults and juveniles.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Osteoderms and small skin ossicles preserved in life position in marine mudstone; no keratin, colour or gut contents survive.

specimenCards.title: NHMUK PV R1111 · lectotype
specimenCards.description: A near-complete skull and skeleton with armour in place, collected by James Harrison in the late 1850s and described by Richard Owen in 1861. It was designated lectotype in 1994 after Owen's original type proved to be a theropod knee joint.
specimenCards.meta: Charmouth · Charmouth Mudstone Formation · Natural History Museum, London

specimenCards.title: Bristol, Cambridge and Charmouth specimens
specimenCards.description: BRSMG Ce12785 in Bristol is a second near-complete adult; CAMSM X39256 in Cambridge is a partial juvenile; the well-preserved skeleton found in 2000 and displayed at Charmouth remains in private hands. Together they underpin the 2020–2021 redescription.
specimenCards.meta: Black Ven, Charmouth · same formation and age as the lectotype

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Complete skulls, articulated skeletons and osteoderm rows preserved in natural position from adults and juveniles.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: Limb proportions indicate habitual quadrupedality; tooth form and jaw geometry indicate low browsing with a simple bite; the armour pattern anchors reconstructions of early thyreophoran evolution.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Keratin coverings of the armour, colour, growth series beyond a few juveniles, geographic range outside Dorset, and the exact position at the base of Thyreophora.
